claims.text: The dynamic mechanical behavior of as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily controlled by temperature- and strain-rate-dependent dislocation mobility.
At low temperatures and high strain rates, enhanced dislocation drag elevates the flow stress of FeNiCrMn.
At low temperatures and high strain rates, limited dynamic recovery elevates the flow stress of FeNiCrMn.
At elevated temperatures, thermally activated cross-slip lowers the flow stress of FeNiCrMn.
At elevated temperatures, dynamic recovery lowers the flow stress of FeNiCrMn toward quasi-static levels.
The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy retains an inherent strength-ductility balance without compositional or phase modification.
Temperature and strain rate will be varied from 300 to 800 K and from 10^-3 to about 10^1 s^-1 in tensile and compressive tests.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can track evolving dislocation density during the proposed tests.
Post-mortem TEM will be used to evaluate dislocation structures, heterogeneity, and evidence of recovery.
Dislocation density and mobility evolve with temperature and strain rate.
Plastic deformation can be controlled by dislocation slip and can be closely related to dislocation density.
Thermal activation modulates cross-slip and recovery in FeNiCrMn.
Increasing strain rate increases the effectiveness of dislocation drag in FeNiCrMn.
Flow stress will increase overproportionally under the combination of low temperature and high strain rate.
Flow stress will soften as temperature increases or strain rate decreases.
A hyperbolic-sinusoidal Arrhenius-type model can represent the relationship among temperature, strain rate, and flow stress over hot-deformation conditions.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to 300-800 K and strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^1 s^-1.
Failure to observe both the predicted flow-stress trends and a correlation between dislocation behavior and dynamic response would falsify the hypothesis.
